We just learned more about Trump’s Venezuela oil deal, and here’s everything you need to know:

4. This deal creates a board designed to be shielded from oversight and accountability. Trump’s own Treasury Secretary wasn’t able to give Congress basic answers or audits when he testified about Venezuela just last month. But we should blindly trust them now?

items.t: Brilliant Badenoch, Four Pence Off Gherkins and a Chancellor Left Exposed John Healey stood up today promising "breathing space now, fresh hope for the future.…
items.tx:
Brilliant Badenoch, Four Pence Off Gherkins and a Chancellor Left Exposed

John Healey stood up today promising "breathing space now, fresh hope for the future." When Kemi Badenoch rose to respond, she dismantled the claim with a single line: this is a budget for getting by, not for getting on. In eleven words, she exposed what fifty minutes of Treasury rhetoric had tried to obscure. A government managing decline and calling it relief.

Badenoch's sharpest moment was also her simplest. Healey had announced £100 energy payments, an extension of the electricity VAT cut, and business rates relief, dressed as a serious response to household pressure. Badenoch's verdict: "Instead, we got 4p off gherkins." The line lands because it exposes the absurdity. A country facing diesel at £2 a litre and gas storage at a third full heading into winter was offered a rounding error and told to be grateful. Badenoch did not need to shout to make the gap visible. She simply held the promise next to the policy and let the distance speak.

She was equally precise on the fiscal claims underneath the theatre. Healey insisted his Budget met the government's own fiscal rules and left £15 billion of headroom by 2029/30, the same confident arithmetic his predecessor Reeves offered before her own numbers moved against her. Badenoch was unimpressed, and rightly so. Headroom quoted four years out, in a Budget delivered against a backdrop of £14 billion in additional forecast debt interest this year alone, is not a cushion. It is a hope dressed up as a forecast, and Badenoch's refusal to accept it at face value was the correct instinct from an opposition that has watched this exact promise fail once already under this government.

Her challenge on enterprise was the one Healey will find hardest to answer honestly. He pointed to new money through the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank, business rates changes, and tax incentives for company founders, and called it a plan to unleash British enterprise. Badenoch's response cut straight through the announcement to the arithmetic underneath it: none of it touches the underlying costs already crushing employers. A tax incentive for founders means little to a business still absorbing last year's National Insurance rise, this year's minimum wage increase, and a wholesale energy bill that has doubled since the Iran crisis began. You cannot unleash enterprise with one hand while taxing its costs with the other, and Badenoch was the only person in the chamber prepared to say so plainly.

Badenoch also went after breathing space itself as a concept, asking how much room Britain genuinely has left when borrowing costs, debt interest and the overall tax burden are all moving in the same direction at once. It is the right question, because breathing space implies slack somewhere in the system, and nothing in Healey's own figures suggests any exists. A Chancellor claiming headroom while debt interest rises by £14 billion in a single year is not managing a surplus of room. He is managing its absence, and hoping nobody checks the working.

What made the performance outstanding was its discipline. Badenoch did not need to invent a crisis or raise her voice to find one. Sharp, witty, and relentlessly on point, she read Healey's own numbers back to him and let the contradiction do the damage itself. A government promising fresh hope, offering 4p off gherkins, and calling £15 billion of headroom security rather than wishful thinking has handed the opposition leader everything she needs to make the case against it. Badenoch made that case, and made it look easy.

items.tx:
II- Situation on Donbas 🇺🇦 (eastern) front

Unlike the southern front, where the situation improved for the Ukrainian army in 2026, the eastern front has not seen any such improvement. However, the Ukrainians can still be satisfied by the slowing of the Russian advance and the recent stabilization of the front near Sloviansk.

In early 2026, the Ukrainians managed to disengage from Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad—since they still held numerous positions in those areas. Even so, intense Russian pressure—exerted by four armies (the 29th, 51st, 41st, and 8th) along a 50-kilometer front—has allowed Russian forces to advance to the outskirts of Dobropilla. The offensive toward the western administrative borders of the Donbas has been halted, and the push toward Druzhkivka has been temporarily repelled.

That said, Russian forces have advanced toward Dobropilla and are carrying out deep infiltrations, reaching the city center and beyond. The city is of critical importance; more significantly, its capture could potentially serve as a springboard for an offensive toward Barvinkove, striking behind the Ukrainian strongholds in the Donbas. While I consider such an offensive unlikely, given the strength of the Ukrainian defensive lines, frequent infiltrations are to be expected.

The battle for Kostiantynivka has now been raging for a year, yet the city has not fallen. I estimate that the Russians hold the advantage in about 50% of the city (though this does not imply firm control or established logistics), while the Ukrainians hold the advantage in about 15%, leaving the remaining 35% contested. For the time being, the advance toward Druzhkivka appears to have slowed, while Ukrainian forces have partially withdrawn from the last positions they held in Chasiv Yar.

Finally, the situation east of the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk—which had deteriorated significantly in 2026—has shown some improvement since September. Ukrainian forces have pushed back the front line near Mykolaivka and Kramatorsk; however, the persistent threat from FPV drones and KAB (guided aerial bombs) remains, having forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of civilians in recent months.

Overall, the military situation in the region is much better than it was in the spring, though it remains tense. The Russians are now within a few kilometers of major cities and new defensive lines, leaving little room for further maneuvering. Consequently, all future combat in the region will likely be frontal. The coming months will be crucial in determining whether the Ukrainian army can successfully stabilize the front and how the Russian advance toward Dobropillia will unfold.

Thank you for following this second update; the next one will cover the situation on the Oskil front.

cd.t: Bibi Hasn’t Won But the Opposition Has Lost

items.tx:
Last night, the exit polls told one story: Netanyahu had lost, but it wasn’t clear who on the other side had won. This morning, the results are telling another. Netanyahu hasn’t won yet, but the change bloc has clearly lost.

I’ve covered politics since the start of the century. I have never seen a camp organize for an election as impeccably, as efficiently and as energetically as the change bloc did. It signed model surplus-vote agreements, so that no leftover votes would go to waste, and ran an unprecedented operation flying Israelis home from abroad to vote. And by the actual count, it ended up with more or less the same number of seats as in the last election.

Demography beat energy, and the message also proved flawed and unsuccessful. The public wasn’t convinced that the war had been a total victory, as Netanyahu claimed, but it also refused to buy the opposition’s claim that it was a total failure. It was repelled by Haredi draft-dodging, but didn’t think the solution was a minority government propped up by draft refusers and anti-Zionists. It was disgusted when ultra-Orthodox protesters chanted “We do not believe in the rule of the Zionists,” but it was just as shocked when “Biladi, Biladi,” the Palestinian national anthem, was sung at the Joint List’s headquarters last night.

Netanyahu’s position changed completely between the release of the exit polls and the arrival of the real results. Last night it seemed clear that Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Likud loyalist, would be ousted and that, one way or another, Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief of staff, would form a minority government. Now, by the criteria Eisenkot himself set, he has lost the legitimacy to form such a government. He promised he wouldn’t rely on the Arab parties’ votes, yet without a majority he would now need the active support of the Joint List, which looks futile and pointless. In post-October 7 Israel, there is no chance that a coalition including six candidates who lost immediate family to Hamas could last long alongside Joint List lawmakers who claim Hamas is simply a charitable organization.

After the 1967 war, Defense Minister Moshe Dayan famously said Israel was waiting for the Arabs to call. In the same spirit, Netanyahu in effect told the change camp before dawn: here’s my phone number, feel free to use it. Yisrael Beiteinu’s Avigdor Lieberman, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Eisenkot now face a dilemma from hell. They can go to another election, one that Israelis abroad will no longer fly home for. They can try to join Netanyahu’s bloc on tough terms, breaking their campaign pledges never to sit with him. Or they can beg the Islamist Ra’am and the Joint List, now drunk on their success, for support.

And one final note: for the entire campaign, we searched for a third bloc, a centrist unity bloc between Netanyahu and his rivals. Candidates included Benny Gantz and former UN Ambassador Gilad Erdan, former general Ofer Winter and economist Yaron Zelekha, former Culture Minister Hili Tropper and who even remembers who else. They all collapsed, evaporated or vanished. And now it turns out the unity bloc may have been the Arab parties all along. Their historic, almost hysterical turnout, at rates that will need careful examination, shattered both sides’ dreams of a 61-seat majority. It reminded Jews on both sides that, after years of division, they may have to learn to sit together after all.

items.tx:
💡MOSSADIL COMMENTARY:
THE ARROGANCE OF THE ANTI-BIBI MOVEMENT

There is a lesson from this election that goes far beyond Benjamin Netanyahu.

For years, a large part of Israel’s opposition has built its political identity around one central objective: Bibi must go.

That may be an effective slogan. It is not a governing philosophy.

You cannot build an entire political movement around opposition to one man, spend an election telling voters primarily who they should reject, and then be surprised when millions of Israelis ask a very basic question:

What exactly are you offering instead?

That is where I believe the arrogance of the anti-Bibi movement became its greatest political weakness.

It operated as though opposition to Netanyahu was itself enough to create a majority. As though the public’s concerns about security, Jewish identity, Iran, Judea & Samaria, the Palestinians and the future character of the state were secondary to the question of Netanyahu’s personality.

But elections have a way of exposing political echo chambers.

The counting is still underway, and the final coalition picture remains unresolved. Early results and exit polls have shown neither major bloc comfortably reaching the 61 seats required to govern on its own.

Whatever the final numbers are, the political choices made after this election may matter almost as much as the results themselves.

Because Netanyahu’s opponents now face a decision that voters will remember.

Do they attempt to build a broad Zionist government with people they profoundly disagree with politically?

Or does removing Netanyahu remain such an overriding objective that they would rather depend on parties outside the Zionist political consensus?

That question became impossible to ignore last night.

At Joint List headquarters, supporters were filmed singing “Biladi, Biladi,” the Palestinian national anthem.

People can interpret that scene however they choose. But politically, opposition leaders should understand exactly how it will be viewed by a very large portion of the Israeli public.

These are Israelis who serve in the IDF, send their children to reserve duty, bury friends and relatives, live through rockets and wars, and may disagree fiercely with Netanyahu.

Many of them are not ideological Likud voters.

Some are centrists. Some are traditional Labor voters. Some desperately want new leadership.

But asking those voters to accept a government whose survival depends on parties whose supporters celebrate an election result by singing the Palestinian national anthem is not a minor political detail.

It is a decision that will have to be defended.

And there is now another issue hanging over the election.

Police arrested three suspects in the Negev on suspicion of attempting to bribe voters to support Ra’am. Investigators say they discovered envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash and Ra’am ballot slips.

That does not prove that Arab turnout was fraudulent. It does not prove a nationwide conspiracy. It certainly does not justify declaring the election stolen before investigators establish the facts.

But it is serious.

And every credible allegation should be investigated completely, wherever it leads.

What opposition leaders do now will therefore be watched extremely closely.

This is where political wisdom matters.

There are enormous disagreements inside Israel’s Zionist majority. There are people on the center, right and left who disagree about Netanyahu, judicial reform, settlements, religion and state, the war and almost everything else.

But they also share something fundamental: they see the continued existence and security of a Jewish and democratic State of Israel as the starting point of the political conversation.

A responsible political system should be capable of finding cooperation somewhere inside that enormous spectrum.

The mask has slipped completely, revealing an entrenched managerial syndicate trembling at the first genuine taste of their own medicine.

Consider the spectacle unfolding in federal courtrooms across this country. James Comey, the towering figurehead of bureaucratic narcissism who treated the director’s chair at the FBI as his personal pulpit, now sits exposed before the law, trapped under the weight of criminal indictments for unauthorized disclosures and congressional deception. The man who demanded absolute reverence from the public proved incapable of adhering to the basic statutes he spent a career wielding against his enemies.

Beside him in the dock stand the architects of the Foreign Influence Task Force. These ex-FBI officials spent years lecturing the nation about Russian subversion while actively conspiring to bury the Hunter Biden laptop and subsequently lying to congressional investigators under oath. They coordinated suppression campaigns, misled lawmakers, and abused their clearances to safeguard their preferred political dynasty. The stench of their deception is now documented on official criminal dockets.

Turn your gaze to the halls of Congress, where Eric Swalwell remains the living emblem of institutional decay. An elected representative compromised by an operative of the Chinese Communist Party was never expelled or held to account by his party; he was elevated, shielded, and paraded as a defender of national security. The left treats foreign espionage as a minor clerical error whenever the compromised asset votes reliably for the party line.

When you strip away their pompous academic rhetoric, you arrive at their actual objective, articulated clearly by Hakeem Jeffries when he declared this week that ICE will not receive a single dime. They demand that American citizens surrender their earnings, obey every administrative diktat, and accept stagnant wages, while criminal cartels and foreign nationals breach sovereign borders with complete impunity. They despise the working citizens who fund this nation, and they intend to disarm the agencies that protect them.

Connect these realities. The weaponization of the intelligence community, the systematic deception of voters, the compromise with foreign adversaries, and the deliberate dismantling of borders are coordinated maneuvers of a predatory elite. For eight years, they believed their control over Washington gave them permanent immunity from consequence.

They are terrified right now because the machinery of justice is finally applying the law without prejudice. The investigators are facing subpoenas; the leakers are facing grand juries; the architects of censorship are running to defense attorneys.

items.tx:
Striking Aden airport proves the Houthis aren’t worried about retaliation. They want it. Escalation is their currency, and retaliation is how they recruit and mobilize; it’s a win-win, in victory and in loss.

The only real threat to their balance of power is the loss of access to the western coast, and it all starts with Hodeidah, which so far has been unchallenged.

The international community must reverse the Stockholm process, as the Houthis have not fulfilled their side of the bargain on Taiz and have completely destroyed any fair governance process in Hodeidah, not to mention the manipulation of humanitarian aid, fuel, and exploitation of the city.
